# Ревизия вопросов: редакция 2026-10-25

Основание: поручение пользователя «давай исправим правила в проекте если нужно и инструкции кординатора», чат 01a173ad-84a8-7523-8177-930a3f773658. Scope: организация уже разрешённой exact2000 ревизии. Цель остаётся 2000 качественно проверенных вопросов.

## Приоритет и переход

Эта редакция явно заменяет противоречащие ей процедурные дополнения старых pinned process, method-pilot, packet-format и bootstrap/task prompts: exact-four literal calls, обязательный whole-output аудит всех tool results, повторное чтение неизменившихся политик, ручной пересчёт журналов и one-card-only scheduling. Она не отменяет содержательные требования этих документов и канонических GAME_SPEC/question-catalog, формат доказательств карточки и ограничения источников.

Координатор завершает уже начатый атомарный результат по его текущему контракту. Затем один раз записывает новую process revision и границу применения в своём существующем manifest, сохраняя ownership, CURRENT, hashes и указатели на историю. Не создавать отдельный migration-проект и не переписывать старые frozen artifacts. Новый порядок действует только для последующих поручений. Исторические FAIL/HOLD, израсходованные попытки и циклы не обнуляются; старые карточки автоматически не переоткрываются.

Для уже ожидающего READONLY ACK исполнителя координатор посылает одно явное START с этой редакцией, точными ID и границами записи. Это разрешённая пользователем смена процедурного контракта; ещё один bootstrap и запрос human GO не нужны. Действующие preservation-only/second-compaction STOP не снимаются. Передача ownership/lease по-прежнему отдельный проверяемый переход. Делегирование, новые чаты, сообщения, merge/deploy допустимы только в пределах имеющейся авторизации; изменение этой политики не расширяет её.

## Компактное поручение и доказательства исполнения

- Поручение: роль, 3 конкретных ID пилота одной темы, baseline, process revision, разрешённые пути, ссылки на content policy и сохранённые источники, формат результата и критерий остановки. Историю и полный checkpoint не копировать.
- Обязательные применимые правила прочитать один раз за revision. Независимые read-only вызовы объединять. Порядок вызовов, оболочка JavaScript, cat/sed/awk и количество outer calls не являются gates качества.
- Идентичность и ownership проверять один раз при назначении/переходе поддерживаемым инструментом и фактическим returned thread ID. Исходные вызовы/журналы сохраняются. Их ручная реконструкция нужна только при конкретном несовпадении, а не при каждом поручении.
- Технические проверки возвращают компактные PASS/FAIL, проверенные ID/revision и путь к полному результату. Проекция вывода не является дефектом, если необходимые факты доступны и полный результат сохранён. Недостающие исходные данные нельзя объявлять прочитанными: дочитать именно недостающий контекст.
- Автор и reviewer лично читают полный текст каждой назначенной карточки и необходимые полные контексты источников. Компактный технический вывод не заменяет содержательное чтение и не превращает чужой PASS в собственную проверку.
- Автоматизировать schema/hash/preimage/frozen-field/link checks существующими helpers; не строить новый универсальный audit framework в контентном цикле. Ошибка checker не равна дефекту карточки. Изолировать конкретную ошибку и её evidence; не повторять неизменившийся неуспешный вызов более двух раз. Неподтверждённый gate остаётся открытым для затронутых ID, остальные могут продвигаться.

## Работа пакетами без общего барьера

- Первый пилот — до 3 ещё не обработанных ID одной темы. Одна карточка остаётся атомарной единицей применения, вердикта и зачёта; пакет — единица поручения и повторного использования контекста.
- Максимум 2 активных авторских пакета, 1 независимый reviewer и 2 пакета в очереди READY. Это потолок, а не требование создавать новых исполнителей. Использовать действующие разрешённые чаты и модели.
- Автор предварительно проверяет наличие сохранённого контекста/доступность источников и обрабатывает ID по очереди. Готовые карточки передаёт сразу; HOLD одного ID не задерживает остальные. Предварительный поиск входит в тот же лимит попыток конкретного claim, не создаёт новый бюджет.
- Сохранённые источники переиспользовать по индексу. При недоступности остаётся прежний лимит: одна попытка и одна официальная альтернатива, затем HOLD конкретного claim. Никаких обходов доступа, третьего источника для исчерпанного claim или сброса истории через новое имя/чат.
- Независимый reviewer проверяет каждый ID, не выборку. До применения сверить preimage; до зачёта independent verdict должен соответствовать точному CURRENT/hash и должны пройти минимальные affected checks. Порядок INITIAL/apply сохранять по действующему content contract; нельзя зачесть неприменённое предложение.
- На содержательный дефект — один адресный fix-cycle и FINAL того же reviewer по новой версии и затронутым зависимостям. Сохранять уже израсходованные циклы. Неустранённый дефект — HOLD с причиной/следующим действием; третьей полной ревизии нет.
- Координатор сверяет evidence детерминированно, не повторяет полную содержательную проверку. QA для общего diff можно объединить, сохраняя связь результата с каждым точным ID/hash. READY, bootstrap и структурный PASS дают ноль зачтённых вопросов.
- После пилота при сохранённом качестве и достаточном контексте допустим пакет 5–10 ID. Это не отменяет compaction fences: насыщенный исполнитель завершает только разрешённый уже начатый атомарный результат и передаёт остальные ID без повторной обработки.

## Учёт результата и остановок

Использовать проекцию существующего manifest/checkpoint по [context-efficiency.md](context-efficiency.md), не второй статусный реестр. Показывать компактно: process revision, текущие ID/этап, accepted delta, HOLD с конкретными причинами, следующий шаг, ссылки на evidence. Все прежние raw evidence сохранять по ссылкам, не тащить в каждый handoff.

На первом пилоте измерить elapsed time, число реально зачтённых ID, HOLD, содержательные и процедурные возвраты, время bootstrap/ожидания/проверки. Токены учитывать только если runtime их сообщает; неизвестное — null, cached/uncached не смешивать. Не обещать ускорение без сравнения. Низкое число HOLD само по себе не показатель качества.

Через 30 минут без нового готового результата диагностировать одно узкое место и изменить следующий шаг в разрешённых пределах. Не прерывать обязательную проверку, не снижать quality gates, не начинать очередной аудит всей истории. При неизменном blocker ждать события/изменения условия, не генерировать ACK/status snapshots. Существующие wait cursors и компактный handoff сохраняются.

## Шаблон инструкции координатору

> После завершения текущего атомарного результата введи process revision 2026-10-25 из этого файла. Сохрани текущие claims, CURRENT, исторические HOLD/FAIL и receipts. Для следующего разрешённого автора: один START на пилот до 3 untouched ID одной темы; baseline, разрешённые пути и source index. Проверь каждый ID независимым reviewer, один fix-cycle максимум, зачёт только точного проверенного CURRENT. Не повторяй bootstrap/exact-four/whole-tool-output audits; технические проверки выполняй helpers с краткой сводкой. Передавай готовые ID без ожидания HOLD-соседей. После пилота сообщи accepted delta, elapsed, причины HOLD и оставшийся bottleneck. Не меняй модели, не переоткрывай исчерпанные claims и не расширяй число исполнителей без существующей авторизации.
# Контекст текущего среза

Читай для длинной задачи, batch-работы, после первого compaction или перед handoff.

- Один согласованный change/связный проверяемый срез — одна исполнительная сессия. Follow-up оставляй в ней, пока результат не завершён; независимая фича получает новый scope. При насыщении контекста уже разрешённой незавершённой задачи создай одного заменяющего исполнителя в прежнем scope, передай ownership и прекрати работу старого. Это не расширяет полномочия; независимый новый чат требует запроса пользователя.
- После первого compaction зафиксируй scope, проверенные факты и оставшиеся gates; сократи срез до уже начатого результата, не загружай соседние пакеты. После второго заверши только текущий атомарный результат, начатые обязательные проверки, сохранение и handoff; не начинай новый batch. Более строгий preservation-only fence сохраняется; не прерывай проверку только ради счётчика.
- Handoff: цель/change ID, branch/SHA и spec revision, сделано/проверено, следующий шаг, blocker/вопрос, ownership/ресурсы и ссылки на evidence. Не копируй историю, логи и выполненные чеклисты. Передача роли нужна при смене ownership или остановке, а не после каждой карточки.
- Вход — проекция существующего актуального manifest: change/ID, revision/hashes, ownership/границы записи, стадия, действующие fences, evidence, следующий шаг и критерий завершения. `python3 tools/manifest_view.py <manifest.json> <JSON-pointer> ...` выводит выбранные поля и SHA исходника без записи; например `/CURRENT /claimsOwner /currentWork`. Историю открывай по конкретному расхождению, не переноси закрытые поля в очередной handoff; исходные artifacts сохраняй.
- Читай только skill текущей фазы и reference по триггеру, один раз за неизменную revision. Объединяй независимые read-only вызовы; выводи сводку и нужные ошибки. При расхождении сначала установи новую revision. Полные логи/evidence остаются по ссылкам.
- Проверки повторяй после относящейся к ним правки, новой ошибки или обязательного gate. Существующие quality/release/visual/audio/device/human gates не ослабляй. Ожидание и курсоры — по [coordination.md](coordination.md); неизменившийся blocker не требует ACK или перезаписи snapshot.

Каталог SHALL применять единые критерии трёх уровней. Easy SHALL проверять широко известный взрослой аудитории факт, включая знания, широко распространённые внутри большой демографической или культурной группы; medium SHALL быть вероятно решаем игроком, знакомым с конкретной тематикой, и существенно труднее для игрока вне неё; hard SHALL требовать специфического знания либо содержательной логики. Каждый вопрос MUST оставаться однозначным, а его неверные варианты MUST быть правдоподобными и позволять игроку без точного знания по возможности сузить выбор без явно абсурдных дистракторов.

- **WHEN** редактор проверяет easy-вопрос
- **THEN** большинство взрослых либо широкая релевантная группа может знать ответ без специальной подготовки, а игрок без знания видит несколько грамматически и смыслово допустимых вариантов

#### Scenario: Medium-вопрос
- **WHEN** редактор проверяет medium-вопрос
- **THEN** знакомый с темой игрок, скорее всего, узнаёт ответ, а игрок вне темы не получает его только из очевидной несостоятельности остальных вариантов

- Одна задача — 10–20 конкретных ID одной темы, один baseline SHA, один авторский результат.

- Один координатор ведёт очередь и интеграцию; один автор готовит конкретную часть; другой человек/агент
  независимо проверяет получившийся CURRENT. Координатор выполняет adjudication и проверку
  согласованности вердиктов, но не делает третью полную содержательную ревизию.
- Применение точного patch и сохранение выполняет координатор обычными инструментами.
  Отдельный opaque-editor или capture-чат нужен только при конкретной технической необходимости,
  а не как обязательный этап для каждой карточки.
- До получения первого полностью завершённого пакета не запускать новую волну авторов.

  очередь ожидающих независимого ревью — не более двух пакетов. Сначала разгружать её.
- Новые чаты/сообщения — только при имеющейся авторизации. При разрешённом запуске:
  автор и механическая работа — GPT-6 Luna/medium; координатор и независимый читатель —
  GPT-6.1 Sol/medium. Не менять модель существующих чатов без отдельного основания.

Одно короткое поручение: цель, список ID, baseline commit, разрешённые пути,
ссылка на требования, индекс сохранённых источников, формат результата, проверка и критерий остановки.

> сложность и смысловые пересечения с релевантными соседями. Сохрани ID/topic/difficulty/key.
> Исправляй только содержательные или языковые дефекты, не переписывай удачный текст ради
> отличия от baseline. Верни patch и manifest: READY, FIX или HOLD по каждому ID.
> Для каждого решения дай конкретное основание и точный locator. Передай готовую часть,
> даже если остальные ID заблокированы. После одного адресного исправления спорные карточки
> вынеси в HOLD; не продолжай бесконечный поиск.

## Источники и доказательства

- Сначала открыть сохранённый первичный контекст по индексу; не скачивать его повторно
  только из-за нового исполнителя. Независимый читатель действительно читает контекст,
  а не наследует авторский PASS.
- Проверять утверждения всех вариантов и заметок. HTTP 200, hash и наличие URL доказывают
  получение файла, но не достоверность текста. Шаблонное «source supports note» не является основанием.
- На недоступный URL: одна ограниченная попытка плюс один официальный альтернативный путь.
  Неполный ответ, challenge, ошибка TLS/DNS или timeout — диагностический результат.
  Затем HOLD конкретного утверждения и точный запрос источника. Не обходить ограничения доступа.
- Общий полный первичный материал сохранять один раз с URL, датой, SHA и locator.
  В карточках — ссылки на этот материал и конкретные основания; не дублировать raw
  в каждом пакете/чате. Сохранность ранее требуемых полных контекстов не ослабляется.
- Существующие шесть групп полей, отдельные основания для вариантов/заметок и frozen hashes
  сохраняются. Формировать hashes и проверять схему инструментом, а не ручным переписыванием.
  Проза нужна для смысла решения, не для пересказа хэшей и маршрута Git.
- Никогда не засчитывать HOLD, structural-only, PASSready или авторский FIX как завершённый CURRENT.

## Независимая проверка и завершение

1. Автор сохраняет patch, точные before/after hashes и доказательства; READY/FIX отделяет от HOLD.
2. Координатор сверяет preimage с текущим файлом, применяет только разрешённые ID атомарно.
   Drift одного ID возвращает только этот ID на сверку; весь пакет заново не открывается.
3. Независимый читатель проверяет точный CURRENT целиком, первичные контексты и релевантных соседей.
   Его результат привязан к hash карточки и содержит конкретный PASS либо дефект.
4. На дефект допускается один адресный fix-cycle; после правки проверяется новая карточка
   и затронутые зависимости. Не перечитывать неизменившиеся другие карточки.
   Неразрешённый дефект — HOLD с владельцем следующего действия, не новое бесконечное поручение.
5. Координатор сопоставляет авторский и независимый результат, разрешает расхождения явно,
   проверяет инварианты/полноту и сохраняет commit. Зачёт увеличивается только для
   уникальных ID с доказанной актуальной версией и пройденными нужными проверками.
6. В checkpoint добавляется результат пакета. В основной записи остаются актуальные IDs,
   hashes, статусы и ссылки; история хранится в отдельных неизменяемых файлах.
   Не наращивать в одном JSON поля successor01..., coordinatorHistory и копии старых пакетов.
   Миграция старого checkpoint — отдельная работа, не ручное удаление истории.

## Проверки и критерии остановки

- До запуска выбрать affected checks по реальному diff. Для документации — ссылки/структура
  и git diff --check. Для контента — проверка схемы, уникальности ID, frozen key/difficulty,
  preimage/after hashes, полноты ссылок и затронутых контрактов каталога.
- Конкретные команды брать из текущего проекта после чтения их маршрута. Не запускать весь
  каталог, full QA, браузер, сборку или deploy «на всякий случай». Runtime QA, если нужен,
  только muted с самого старта. Автоматическая проверка не заменяет содержательное ревью.
- Через 30 минут без передачи хотя бы одной готовой карточки сохранить короткий checkpoint:
  что мешает, какие ID готовы, какое конкретное следующее действие. Это сигнал сменить маршрут,
  а не снизить требования к качеству или оборвать выполняющуюся обязательную проверку.
- Два одинаковых технических сбоя подряд: сохранить состояние, прекратить повторения
  неизменившегося вызова и сообщить конкретный блокер. Heartbeat не должен бесконечно будить
  сломанный координатор; возобновление требует изменения условия.
- После первого compaction сохранить текущий срез; после второго — только атомарное
  завершение, сохранение и остановка. Преемник получает manifest незавершённого среза,
  а не всю историю. Не создавать преемников ради повторного оформления тех же доказательств.
- wait_threads использовать с сохранённым cursor. Полный read_thread — только для нового
  результата, ошибки или перехода; большие ответы сначала фильтровать, не выводить в контекст.

Это точная форма уже действующих six/four/source/peer требований, а не новая процедура приёмки. Для знакомства со схемой не печатать целиком старые candidate/sourceproof/peer-snapshot. Три файла: `candidate.json`, `sourceproof.json`, `peer-snapshot.json`. В каждом — один и тот же фактический `sourceNativeId`, `topicId`, `cycle`, ID карточки. Native ID подтверждается coordinator по реальному session_meta, а не копируется из task owner. До START никаких записей.

## Хэши: три разных представления

```python
def canonical_sha(value):
    return hashlib.sha256(json.dumps(value, ensure_ascii=False,
        sort_keys=True, separators=(',', ':')).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
def file_sha(path):
    return hashlib.sha256(Path(path).read_bytes()).hexdigest()
def body_sha(text):
    return hashlib.sha256(text.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
```

- Карточка, literal (включая строку), triple и rows: `canonical_sha`.
- Файл: `file_sha`. Не путать с хэшем содержимого строки внутри JSON.
- Полный original tool body, извлечённый по JSON Pointer: `body_sha`. JSON-кавычки и escaping в этот hash не входят.
- Никогда не переписывать hex вручную и не копировать hash между разными представлениями.

## Candidate

`entries[0]` содержит `id`, `topicId`, `sourceOrder`, `status`, `beforeCard`, `beforeHash`, `proposedCard`, `afterHash`, `fieldGroups`.

`status` — `READY_FOR_INDEPENDENT_REVIEW` либо точный `HOLD`; quality credit всегда0. Before — действительный preimage текущего назначения. Frozen ID/topic/order/difficulty/numeric key проверить по selection. Labels не заморожены глобально; править хороший текст без конкретного дефекта нельзя.

Использовать только dict-форму `fieldGroups`: ровно шесть ключей, каждый с вычисленными `beforeCanonicalSHA256` / `afterCanonicalSHA256`:

```python
def groups(card):
    return {
      'prompt_ordered_answers_key': {
        'prompt': card['prompt'],
        'answers': [a['text'] for a in card['answers']],
        'correctIndex': card['correctIndex']},
      'explanation': card['explanation'],
      **{'note'+str(k): a['note'] for k,a in enumerate(card['answers'])}}
```

## Sourceproof

`rawSources[]`: `path`, `url`, `sha256` (реальный file SHA), `captureReadProvenance`, `locator`. Для JSON-container также `completeOutputPointer` и `completeOutputSHA256` (= body SHA). Для общего capture перечислить все реальные URL/locators; не терять их из-за одинакового file path.

`path` — только существующий устойчивый файл. Не `journal item N`, не `file#pointer`, не URL. JSON Pointer хранится отдельным полем. L280: Etymology
L281: 
L282: Noun
L283: 
L284: Middle English las, lace "a string used to draw together two edges of material," from early French laz (same meaning), from Latin laqueus "noose, snare" — related to 【45†lash entry 3】, 【46†lasso entry 1】
L285: 
L286: Word Origin
L287: When the ancient Romans wanted to trap a small animal, such as a rabbit, they used a loop of light rope laid on the ground in its path. A triggering device was used to tighten the loop around the animal. They called such a loop or noose laqueus, which became laz in early French. The English borrowed it as las in the 14th century. They used it to refer to a cord that holds something together by weaving, as a shoelace.
L288: Finally, it came to mean the delicate fabric made by weaving and knotting thin strands of material.

L287: When the ancient Romans wanted to trap a small animal, such as a rabbit, they used a loop of light rope laid on the ground in its path. A triggering device was used to tighten the loop around the animal. They called such a loop or noose laqueus, which became laz in early French. The English borrowed it as las in the 14th century. They used it to refer to a cord that holds something together by weaving, as a shoelace.
L288: Finally, it came to mean the delicate fabric made by weaving and knotting thin strands of material.

L61: ## Exhibition Overview
L62: From the clothing of ancient Greece to such modern evocations as Madame Grès's emblematic creations and Versace's Neoclassical loincloths, classical dress has profoundly inspired and influenced art and design over the millennia. The exhibition presents clothing, prints, photographs, and decorative works of art, from the eighteenth century onward, to reveal the many ways in which classical dress has become a truly timeless style.
L63: With more than two hundred items on display, including clothing from the Directoire and Empire periods, the exhibition features loans of vintage and contemporary designs from international couture houses and private collectors along with works from the permanent collection of The Costume Institute.
L64: The designers featured include Paul Poiret, Madame Grès, Madeleine Vionnet, Balenciaga, Charles James, Bill Blass, Holly Harp, Gilbert Adrian, Claire McCardell, Jean Patou, Louiseboulanger, Lucile, Lucian Lelong, Pierre Cardin, Elsa Schiaparelli, Yves Saint Laurent, Fortuny, Alexander McQueen, John Galliano, Tom Ford for Gucci and Yves Saint Laurent Rive Gauche, Halston, Molyneux, Christian Dior, Hussein Chalayan, Mary McFadden, Donna Karan, Isabel Toledo, La Perla, Stéphane Rolland for Jean Louis Scherrer, Valentino, Rick Owens, Dolce & Gabbana, Gianni Versace, Tommy Hilfiger, Carolina Herrera, Ralph Rucci, Christian Lacroix, m.r.s., Julien MacDonald for Givenchy, Lainey Keogh, Shelley Fox, Thierry Mugler, Cesare Paciotti, Miuccia Prada, Roberto Cavalli, Arnold Scaasi, Vera Wang, Giorgio Armani, Alberta Ferretti, Emanuel Ungaro, Stavropoulos, Norma Kamali, Douglas Ferguson, Oscar de la Renta for Pierre Balmain, Yohji Yamamoto, Romeo Gigli, Clements Ribeiro, Ann Demeulemeester, Lars Nilsson for Bill Blass, Ronaldus Shamask and Michele Oka Doner, Nicolas Ghesquière for Callaghan, Jean Paul Gaultier, Issey Miyake, Karl Lagerfeld for Chanel, and the costumes created for Isadora Duncan's groundbreaking dance performances.
L65: * * *
L66: 
L67: The exhibition and the accompanying catalogue are made possible by GUCCI.
L68: Additional support for the exhibition has been provided by Condé Nast.
L69: 
L70: * * *
L71: 
L72: [Input] Pandora's Box: The Chiton, Peplos, and Himation
L73: In the absence of any surviving clothing, art and literature provide the only evidence of classical dress, opening a Pandora's Box of confusion and contradiction. The apparel of ancient Greece was, even in its own day, subject to numerous modifications and transformations. In the huge variety of costumes delineated in artworks and categorized by scholars, exceptions are rife and consistency is elusive.
L74: Because specialists of the high classical period of ancient Greece have developed terminology based on a variety of methodologies—art historical, archaeological, and literary—certain discrepancies are perhaps inevitable. However, in every instance, the glossaries are also a simplified system, identifying numerous and specific forms of dress under quite general labels.
L75: In this exhibition, the nomenclature was simplified even further and was based on the structure of the garment rather than any other criteria.
L76: The diversity of women's apparel in ancient Greece can be reduced to three general garment types: the chiton, the peplos, and the himation.
L77: Structurally, the most elemental dress type is the chiton, which is constructed in several ways. The most commonly represented is accomplished by stitching two rectangular pieces of fabric together along either sideseam, from top to bottom, forming a cylinder with its top edge and hem unstitched. The top edges are then sewn, pinned, or buttoned together at two or more points to form shoulder seams, with reserve openings for the head and arms.
L78: The peplos is perhaps a more distinctively Greek garment than the chiton, insofar as the chiton's reductive construction has similarities to apparel types in a number of other cultures and times. However, the peplos has several characteristics that distinguish it from other clothing traditions. Made of one large rectangular piece of cloth, it was formed into a cylinder and then folded along the top, creating an apoptygma, or capelet-like overfold.
L79: Although there are exceptional instances of chitons represented with overfolds, a garment is not a peplos unless it has been draped with an apoptygma. Brooch-like pins attached the back to the front of the garment at either shoulder. The fastening of the shoulders with fibulae is the single defining detail of the peplos.
L80: While there are a number of scarf, veil, shawl, and mantle forms worn by the ancient Greeks, it is the himation, with its range of draping and wrapping possibilities, that has been the most evident source of later evocations of Hellenic dress. The himation was a large cloak, always rectangular, unlike the Roman toga, which had some shaping. Like the toga, however, it appears to have had a variety of cultural meanings, depending on its proportion and how it was worn.
L81: Generally, when worn by women, it was a garment of decorous modesty, but it has been shown on hetærae, or courtesans, as a device for provocation.
L82: The diminishing number of paradigmatic Grecian dress types belies the artistic and literary evidence. But it may be that in the narrowing of types, their potency as carriers of ideals of the antique became even more concentrated over time. It is in the variation and manipulation of a reduced number of basic iconic styles that later artists and contemporary designers have been able to expand on their increasingly inventive interpretations of Grecian dress.
L83: [Input] The Metamorphoses: Classical Transformations and Contemporary Permutations
L84: The richness and variety of the costumes represented in ancient Greek art are the result of simple manipulations of the three basic garment types: the chiton, the peplos, and the himation. The positioning of a waist cinch or a shoulder harness and the removal of a fibula introduced to the ancient wardrobe the possibility of innumerable effects. Over time and through diverse artistic interpretations, these variations have been modified and metamorphosed into an even greater diversity of styles.
L85: Still, the resulting garments retain their connotative relationship to the original historical model.
L86: One of the details that has come to denote the ancient silhouette is the cinching-in with a belt, the zone, that occurred above the natural waistline. In Napoleonic France, this "classical" waistline rose to a point directly under the bustline, even higher than the mid-ribcage level preferred by the ancients. This exaggeration, ubiquitous as a fashion during the Neoclassical period from the 1790s through the 1810s, came to be called the Empire waist.
L87: Unlike the waistline of antiquity, which employed a cinch or belt, the Empire waist was structural with an almost vestigial bodice connected to a floor-length skirt by seaming.
L88: While the chemise dress of the Empire period relied on pattern-cutting to establish the high Neoclassical-style waistline, the fullness of ancient Greek apparel was controlled by the use of bindings and ties. Depictions of double girdling on both the peplos and chiton suggest that one belt pulled in the waist and raised the hemline, thereby creating a kolpos, or blouson, and a second binding, worn over the blouson, established a visible, decorative waistline.
L89: Over the centuries, artists and designers have used double girdling and the blouson to evoke this ancient practice.
L90: Another zone of classical allusion has been the neckline. Antique representations of one-shouldered, breast-baring garments shown on goddesses and Amazons as a specific signifier of their mythic identity are the basis for the association of asymmetrical necklines with Hellenic attire.
L91: Over the two millennia that separate us from the Græco-Roman period, a small number of clothing types have come to represent classical dress. As in ancient Greece, inventive variations of wearing the peplos, chiton, and himation have emerged. Even at a considerable remove from direct reference to specific ancient garment types, such details retain the ability to invoke a classical mode.
L92: 
L93: [Input] Pygmalion's Galatea: Art to Life
L94: The Roman poet Ovid recounted an ancient myth in which Pygmalion, a sculptor disenchanted by mortal women, created an image of feminine perfection. When he became enthralled with his own sculpted ideal, Venus—the Greek Aphrodite—responded to his prayers and brought the statue to life as Galatea.
L95: Through the centuries, art and fashion have achieved their own transformations, adding elements not present in the original garments. Even in the most naturalistic representation of Hellenic dress, subjective and prescribed stylistic qualities are inevitably introduced. In depicting details of ancient Greek attire, later artists and designers have changed, as much as preserved, the actual qualities of ancient garb.
L96: Among the stylizations that have most influenced fashion designers is wet drapery, a term used by art historians to describe fabric that seems to cling to the body in animated folds while revealing the contours of the form beneath. This sculptural style—evidenced in figures from the Classical and Hellenistic periods—has emerged in fashion as a signifier of classicizing intent.
L97: From the nineteenth century to the present, designers have utilized a variety of techniques and materials to replicate its effects.
L98: In some artistic renderings from antiquity, textiles appear fragile, and even ephemeral, qualities that are described in ancient literary texts. Gossamer robes, shawls, and veilings became one of the most potent associations with the antique, as exemplified by the popular use of light mull, a sheer cotton fabric during the Empire period, and also of tulle and chiffon.
L99: The classicizing effect is further underscored if the fabric is white, since there has been a longstanding convention that classical styles should be achromatic. This misconception, thought to derive from the faded and abraded surfaces of originally polychromed Greek statuary and architecture, is perpetuated in fashion to this day.
L100: Drapery of the Classical and Hellenistic periods sometimes appears purely as a foil for nudity, clinging and spiraling around the body. Frequently, trhis effect is a stylistic preference rather than an actual manner of dress or response to natural phenomena. Such animated drapery frequently takes on a schematic form, with fluted edges regularized into a rhythmic pattern of handkerchief-pointed "swallowtail" folds, a characteristic that has inspired fashion designers in the twentieth century.
L101: In Greek art, fabrics are rendered with the texture of both regular folds and irregular pleating. Such differentiated representations have also found expression in later fashion designs. By employing a variety of techniques, designers as disparate as Mariano Fortuny, Madeleine Vionnet, Madame Grès, Mary McFadden, and Norma Kamali have achieved effects redolent of the stylized characteristics of cloth seen in the art of ancient Greece.
L102: [Input] Mythic Details: The Greek Key, Laurels, and the Attributes of Goddesses
L103: Most early post-classical depictions of ancient Grecian themes represent the gods, demi-gods, and mortals in loosely draped, monochromatic robes. If present at all, the only ornamentation is a narrow banded border of braid or embroidery. However, vase paintings, painted sculptures, and ancient literary references provide extensive evidence for the use of decorative embellishments in ancient Greek dress.
L104: A cursory survey of red-and-black figure vase paintings reveals that antique dress was composed of a rich variety of patterned textiles.
L105: Among the most common designs seen in ancient art is the Greek-key pattern, a rectilinear meander. Other abstracted forms of wave patterns, geometric repeats, and palmette friezes were also seen on classical garments, as were more intricate borders depicting animals, birds, and fish as well as complex battle scenes. Nevertheless, such patterns have only rarely been used by later artists or by contemporary designers.
L106: Of all these motifs, the Greek key and wave patterns appear most frequently in designs intended to evoke the antique. In some instances, the key pattern is broken into a discontinuous segmented band, but even this disrupted linear repeat is sufficient to sustain the classical connection.
L107: Although well represented in art, mythological attributes of Olympian deities are less common in fashion. However, the ancient Greek practice of recognizing achievement and bestowing honor through the presentation of a coronet of flowers and leaves was reflected in Neoclassical embroideries and in more recent creations.
L108: Certain details of the coronets originally associated with the presiding deities—laurels for Apollo, olive leaves for Athena, roses for Aphrodite, ivy for Dionysos—are perhaps too esoteric for the purposes of fashion and have generally been obscured. Still, other mythic attributes have continued with their original meanings intact.
L109: Christian Dior, Valentino, Alexander McQueen, and Gianni Versace have incorporated in their designs attributes of Greek goddesses—peacock feathers for Hera, sea foam and shells for Aphrodite, and the aegis (breastplate) for Athena.
L110: Over time, reductive simplicity emerged as a way of conveying an aura of the antique, a strategy that was further developed in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries. Still, patterns and designs from the repertoire of ancient ornament, as well as various attributes of the Olympian deities evoke classical antiquity. Incorporating these elements into their creations, contemporary designers have introduced to fashion the narratives of ancient myth.
L111: In a field characterized by constant change, they have clung to the illusion of an ideal of beauty through the resonant imagery of classical decorative motifs.

L115: Faldilla de silueta sirena, molt cenyida als malucs i a la part superior de les cames. A l'alçada dels genolls la faldilla s'eixampla, mitjançant gaies. La faldilla duu uns enagos interiors que li donen volum, i acaba amb cua.
L116: El punt dóna una imatge orgànica al vestit, creant textura sobre superfícies planes. En aquest vestit, en què hi ha molt domini del patronatge, el teixit de punt crea una superfície texturada.
L117: ### Vocabulari
L118: 
L119: #### Gaia
L120: 
L121: Tros de roba rectangular que s'aplica a un vestit o faldilla per donar el vol necessari, generalment tallada al biaix. En llengua castellana s'anomena “godet”.
L122: 
L123: #### Punt
L124: 
L125: Lligat d’un o més fils que s’entrellacen, trenen o nuen, el qual forma l’element constitutiu d’un teixit, d’un treball de mitja, etc. (DIEC)
L126: 
L127: #### Enagos
L128: 
L129: Peça de vestir interior femenina consistent en una faldilla de roba blanca.
L130: 
L131: ### Firma
L132: #### Novak
L133: 
L134: La dissenyadora Henar Velázquez (Igualada, 1963) va fundar juntament amb Miquel Santacana l'empresa familiar Novak, que confeccionà peces de punt per a dona des de 1963 fins a 2003. El projecte va créixer arrelat a la ciutat d’Igualada i acabà conquistant el mercat internacional amb la creació de dues col·leccions anuals.
L135: La seva impulsora va escollir el nom de la marca arran del ressò de Kim Novak, una de les actrius fetitxe d'Alfred Hitchcock. El tret distintiu de Novak era la moda femenina, així com la innovació i el treball amb punt. Tot i que era difícil competir amb l’alta costura, cal reconèixer la tasca duta terme amb la creació de peces que combinaven a la perfecció modernitat i classicisme, buscant perfils elegants; a més, posava a l’abast del gran públic peces de molta qualitat.
L136: Així mateix, és important destacar la creació de vestits de núvia en punt. "La Novak", com es coneixia popularment, va ser una de les marques comercials amb més carisma i reconeixement internacional de la comarca de l’Anoia.

L140: ### Context
L141: #### 1990-1999
L142: La moda dels anys noranta va ser un fenomen que es caracteritzà pels seus canvis ràpids. No hi havia un estil específic sinó més aviat l’impuls de les persones per marcar la seva individualitat a través de la roba. En línies generals, destacaren com a usuals els pantalons de cintura baixa, els escots prominents, o els jeans, que ja des de la dècada anterior tingueren un gran èxit. Els destenyits i trencats són els més comuns.
L143: Les samarretes curtes fins al melic varen resultar ideals per lluir piercings i tatuatges. Moltes d’aquestes tendències van sorgir en entorns urbans degradats.
L144: A això cal sumar-hi l’aportació dels moviments musicals: el grounge look amb Nirvana com a màxim exponent, proposà pantalons desgastats i camises de quadres; el hip hop, el look underground, o el Rap foren també destacables amb l’aportació de roba ampla i la característica gorra de visera.
L145: Es proposaven models assexuats i un cànon excessivament esvelt, que recordava les dones-nena dels anys vint. Varen ser temps gloriosos per supermodels com Claudia Schiffer, Naomi Campbell, Judit Mascó i Christy Turlington, per esmentar-ne algunes. Això va imposar una norma de cos prim que es va traslladar aviat al comú de les dones i va desencadenar debats i preocupacions per casos d’anorèxia.
L146: Ideològicament, la llibertat sexual tornà a influenciar en la moda, andrògina i uniformada. Són anys de contínua relectura de models de les dècades anteriors, els cinquanta, els seixanta i els setanta, que incloïen postures properes a l’antimoda i estètica popular, i fins i tot més llunyanes com la Belle Époque. La moda en la darrera dècada del segle es caracteritzà per l’extrema senzillesa en contraposició als excessos dels vuitanta, dels quals només romangué el gust pel negre.
L147: En aquests anys es reactivà l’alta costura, que es revestí d’actituds com la provocació i la reacció contra la uniformitat. Va ser una època de consolidació i èxit de cadenes de moda com Gap, Zara – el grup Inditex no només tenia gran implantació a Espanya sinó a tot el món–, Mango o Banana Republic, que trencaren amb la idea de qualitat-preu.
L148: A finals de la dècada va decaure el minimalisme extrem i la uniformitat, al mateix temps que la moda caminà cap a peces més còmodes i juvenils enfront el vestit sastre, i que el fenomen de les top-model havia perdut la seva anterior trascendència.
L149: En els anys noranta i els principis del segle XXI, en la moda espanyola, destaquen noms com Amaya Arzuaga, Duyos y Paniagua, Javier Larraínzar, Armand Basi, Roberto Torretta, Victorio & Lucchino, Antonio Pernas, Ángel Schlesser, Devota y Lomba, etc. També és destacable la dinamització de la moda espanyola a través de l’impuls de les passarel·les, com la Cibeles (Madrid) o la Gaudí (Barcelona).
L150: 
L151: ...
L152: El desenvolupament de la moda durant el segle XX va venir marcat pels diferents esdeveniments històrics. Si a Europa i als Estats Units les dues guerres mundials van ser d’especial rellevància, a Catalunya cal esmentar la successió de diferents règims: monarquia (Alfons XIII, 1902-1931; Juan Carlos I 1975-2014), dictadura (Primo de Rivera, 1923-1930; Francisco Franco, 1939-1975), i república (Segona República, 1931-1939), a més de la Guerra Civil (1936-39).
L153: El segle XX suposà el triomf de la industrialització del sector tèxtil. Amb aquest un espectre de població molt més ampli que l’habitual fins llavors va poder accedir a certs productes d’ús minoritari, fet que accelerarà els canvis en la moda. Això implicà l’aparició i generalització de tendències consumistes en la indumentària, substituïnt les peces sense esperar que es fessin malbé, davant la necessitat creada de tenir el producte que dictava la moda.
L154: En aquest període la firma de les peces garantia el prestigi i reconeixement social de qui les posseïa. Les primeres cases d’alta costura, que ja havien aparegut a les darreries del segle anterior, es consolidaren, com les de Carolina Montagne, la de María Molist, El Dique Flontante o Santa Eulàlia. Malgrat estar restringida a una elit econòmica, l’alta costura seguí marcant la moda i establí tendències.
L155: No obstant, el major impacte social de la moda es produí a través del prêt-à-porter i la producció en sèrie que, tot recollint les tendències de l’alta costura, tingué una gran difusió a través dels mitjans de comunicació (La ilustración española y americana o Blanco y Negro).
L156: Llevat d’algunes excepcions, se seguiren les línies de la moda internacional, especialment franceses en el vestit femení i angleses en el masculí. Això condicionà la manca de reconeixement dels creadors espanyols en el seu país, i com a conseqüència, el poc suport de la indústria. No fou fins la dècada dels anys 1970 i 1980  que es reactivà la indústria i el mercat espanyol amb el sorgiment d’una generació potent de disenyadors i el suport institucional, sobretot durant els anys vuitanta.
L157: Va ser durant la dècada següent, coincidint amb la internacionalització de la moda, quan la indústria local s’expandí fora de les fronteres.

L55: # 1966
L56: Le premier smoking
L57: 
L58: Lié à 【27†Mode】
L59: 
L60: Dans la collection automne-hiver de 1966, Yves Saint Laurent introduit la pièce la plus iconique de son style : le smoking. À l’origine, c’est un vêtement d’homme réservé au fumoir, pièce à laquelle il doit son nom puisque la veste qu’on y portait servait à protéger l’habit de l’odeur du cigare. Le vêtement, de part son usage, était alors exclusivement masculin.
L61: Le smoking Saint Laurent n’est cependant pas la copie d’une pièce masculine. Yves Saint Laurent utilise les codes tout en les adaptant au corps féminin.
L62: 
L63: > Pour une femme, le smoking est un vêtement indispensable avec lequel elle se sentira continuellement à la mode car c’est un vêtement de style et non un vêtement de mode. Les modes passent, le style est éternel.
L64: 
L65: Yves Saint Laurent
L66: Trop novateur, il est boudé dans un premier temps par la clientèle haute couture si bien qu’un seul exemplaire est vendu. Paradoxalement, c’est un succès dans sa version SAINT LAURENT rive gauche. La clientèle plus jeune s’arrache cet ensemble. Le smoking devient alors un classique, Yves Saint Laurent le reprendra dans chacune de ses collections jusqu’en 2002.

L27: #
L28: 
L29: Alexander McQueen – an introduction
L30: 
L31:   * Last updated: 17 April 2024
L32: 
L33: Alexander McQueen was one of the most celebrated fashion designers of his generation, known for his highly original designs that married artistry with exceptional technical ability.
L34: Alexander McQueen (1969 – 2010), known to his friends and family as Lee, was born and educated in London. He left school at 16 to become an apprentice on Mayfair's Savile Row – the historic centre of British menswear tailoring – first at Anderson & Sheppard, and then at Gieves & Hawkes, where he learned traditional tailoring techniques. He later worked as a pattern cutter at the theatrical costumiers Angels & Bermans.
L35: At age 20, McQueen began working as a pattern cutter for the avant-garde, London-based Japanese designer Koji Tatsuno, before moving to Milan to join Romeo Gigli, an Italian designer admired for his understated, romantic designs. McQueen returned to London to complete the prestigious MA in Fashion Design at Central Saint Martins. Already a proficient tailor, here he learned how to be a fashion designer, drawing inspiration from London's history, its world-class museums and emerging BritArt scene.
L36: His graduate collection gained him extensive press coverage, and was purchased in its entirety by the influential fashion stylist Isabella Blow.
L37: 【15†Image†vanda-production-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Suit, Alexander McQueen, It’s a Jungle Out There, Autumn/Winter 1997, designed in Britain, made in Italy. Museum no. T.90:1, 2-2011. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L38: McQueen launched his own label in 1992. He was appointed head designer at Givenchy in 1996, succeeding John Galliano. In December 2000, the Gucci Group (now Kering) acquired a majority stake in McQueen's company, and he continued to serve as creative director. McQueen's occasionally stormy relationship with Givenchy ended in 2001.
L39: 
L40: McQueen's influences
L41: McQueen's work was admired for its highly original blend of subversion and tradition, evident from the outset in his 'Bumster' trousers, sharp frock coats, corroded fabrics, slashed leather and shredded, flesh-revealing lace.
L42: 
L43: > You've got to know the rules to break them. That's what I'm here for, to demolish the rules but to keep the tradition.
L44: 
L45: Alexander McQueen
L46: McQueen's Savile Row training would inform his career: "Everything I do is based on tailoring", he said. This background in precision tailoring, combined with the more improvised dressmaking and draping techniques he learned in the atelier (the highly skilled workshops of couture houses) at Givenchy – paved the way for his innovative experiments with cutting and construction.
L47: > Because I was a tailor, I didn't totally understand softness, or lightness. I learned lightness at Givenchy. I was a tailor at Savile Row. At Givenchy I learned to soften. For me, it was an education. As a designer I could have left it behind. But working at Givenchy helped me learn my craft.
L48: 
L49: Alexander McQueen
L50: 
L51: 【16†Image†vanda-production-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Evening dress, Alexander McQueen, Autumn/Winter 2010, Britain. Museum no. T.110-2011. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L52: One of the defining features of Alexander McQueen's collections was their far-reaching historicism. The 1995 Highland Rape collection was informed by his Scottish heritage, referencing the Highland Clearances of the 18th and 19th centuries, when tenants in the Scottish Highlands were forcefully evicted. McQueen was particularly inspired by the 19th century, drawing frequently on Victorian Gothic. Radical re-presentations of historical narratives continued throughout his career.
L53: "I like to challenge history", he stated in the 2008 BBC television series British Style Genius, emphasising the semi-autobiographical nature of some of his historical subject choices.
L54: 【17†Image†vanda-production-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Dress, Alexander McQueen, Plato's Atlantis, Spring/Summer 2010, Britain. Museum no. T.11-2010. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L55: 
L56: As a student, McQueen would visit the V&A at least once a week, to go through the archives and take inspiration from the Museum's diverse collections – from textiles to woodcarvings. He said, "The collections at the V&A never fail to intrigue and inspire me".
L57: McQueen was also inspired by global influences. Africa, China, India and Turkey were all places that sparked his imagination, though Japan was perhaps the most thematically and stylistically significant. The Japanese 【18†kimono】 was a garment that McQueen endlessly reconfigured in his collections.
L58: McQueen's exploration of polarities – man versus machine, or nature versus technology – was a recurring theme in his work. His collections often featured fashions that took their forms and raw materials from the natural world, such as the 【19†Mussel Shell Bodice】 from VOSS (Spring/Summer 2001), or the 【20†Bird's Nest】 headdress developed by Mcqueen's longstanding collaborators Philip Treacy and Shaun Leane for The Widows of Culloden collection (Autumn/Winter 2006).
L59: 
L60: On the catwalk
L61: McQueen was known for the dramatic intensity of his fashion shows, inspired by performance art and theatre.
L62: His spectacular catwalk presentations included the likes of VOSS (Spring/Summer 2001), which was centred around a glass box that resembled a padded cell in a psychiatric hospital, Scanners (Autumn/Winter 2003), where models traversed wind tunnels suspended above the runway, and The Widows of Culloden (Autumn/Winter 2006), where the model Kate Moss appeared as an ethereal apparition within a glass pyramid, echoing a 19th-century stage trick, 'Pepper's Ghost【21†'†en.wikipedia.org】.
L63: In 2009, Plato's Atlantis (Spring/Summer 2010) became the first fashion show to be live streamed on the Internet, via fashion website SHOWstudio.
L64: 【22†Image†vanda-production-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Pepper's Ghost of Kate Moss wearing a silk organza dress, Alexander McQueen, The Widows of Culloden, Autumn/Winter 2006. Art direction by Baillie Walsh. Image: courtesy of Baillie Walsh
L65: During his lifetime, McQueen featured in two V&A Fashion in Motion events – live catwalk presentations staged against the beautiful backdrop of the Museum. The first, in June 1999, showcased designs from McQueen's 【23†Spring/Summer 1999 collection】, while the second, in October 2001, celebrated the years of collaboration between McQueen and the jewellery designer 【24†Shaun Leane】.
L66: By then, McQueen's reputation was such that over 3,000 people gathered in the Museum's grand entrance, hoping to see the event.
L67: Collaborations
L68: McQueen worked with a loyal, close-knit team and was known for his ability to recognise talent in others, whether jeweller, milliner or filmmaker. For his spectacular catwalk shows, he commissioned an array of one-off creations, not intended for production. To realise this vision, he worked with a diverse range of materials and craftspeople – from skilled woodcarvers to 'plumassiers' (feather workers), embroiderers to leather workers.
L69: As well as his longstanding collaboration with Shaun Leane, McQueen worked closely with the milliner 【25†Philip Treacy】.
L70: 【26†Image†vanda-production-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Bird’s Nest headdress, The Widows of Culloden, Philip Treacy and Shaun Leane for Alexander McQueen.
L71: 
L72: Projects and accolades
L73: Between 2000 and 2010, McQueen opened stores in London, New York, Los Angeles, Las Vegas and Milan. His collaborative projects included working with PUMA on a special line of trainers; launching McQ, a younger, lower priced diffusion collection (2006); releasing the fragrances Kingdom (2003) and MyQueen (2005); and a collection of cosmetics for MAC (2007) inspired by the actress Elizabeth Taylor in her film role as Cleopatra.
L74: McQueen's accolades included being awarded the title of British Designer of the Year by the British Fashion Council four times between 1996 and 2001. In 2003, he was awarded a CBE for his services to the fashion industry and also named International Designer of the Year by the Council of Fashion Designers of America. Celebrities including Nicole Kidman, Sarah Jessica Parker, Bjork and Lady Gaga all wore his designs.
L75: In February 2010, McQueen was found dead in his London flat. Over 1,000 guests attended his memorial service. His final, unfinished collection (Autumn/Winter 2010) was completed by Sarah Burton, McQueen's Head of Womenswear since 2000.
L76: The career of Alexander McQueen was celebrated in the exhibition, 【27†Alexander McQueen: Savage Beauty】, first held at New York's Metropolitan Museum of Art in summer 2011, where it attracted 661,509 visitors over three months. It subsequently became the V&A's most visited exhibition, receiving 493,043 visitors during its 21-week run in 2015.

After years of military and civilian uniforms, sartorial restrictions and shortages, Dior offered not merely a new look but a new outlook. L195: Born and raised in Normandy, France, Dior moved with his parents to Paris when he was ten. After studying political science, he served in the military. His design career did not begin until 1935, when he returned to Paris and began selling sketches. The designer Robert Piguet hired him in 1938. During World War II, Dior served in the south of France, then returned again to Paris in 1941 and worked for Lucien Lelong at a much larger design house. L196: In 1946, backed by textile manufacturer Marcel Boussac, he opened his own house. L197: Dior helped to restore a beleaguered postwar Paris as the capital of fashion. Each of his collections throughout this period had a theme. Spring 1947 was “Carolle” or “figure 8,” a name that suggested the silhouette of the new look with its prominent shoulders, accentuated hips, and small waist. The spring 1953 collection, dubbed “Tulip,” featured an abundance of floaty, flowery prints. L198: Spring 1955’s “A-line,” with its undefined waist and smooth silhouette that widened over the hips and legs, resembled a capital “A.” Some of Dior’s designs simulated Second Empire and other historical styles, but he was also creating menswear, trompe-l’oeil detailing, and soft-to-hard juxtapositions, making them part of the modern wardrobe. By his final collections, Dior, feeling the need for a more limber 【39†silhouette】 and lifestyle, was designing chemises, narrow tunics, and sari-like wraps. L199: Together with his partner Jacques Rouet, Dior pioneered license agreements in the fashion business. By 1948, he had arranged lucrative licensing deals for fur, stockings, and perfumes, which not only generated revenue but also made him a household name. While the House of Dior is still a thriving business today, Dior’s untimely death in 1957 left the fashion world without a great dictator of style. L200: Christian Dior designed under his own name for only a decade, but his influence will be felt for many years to come. L29: Alexander McQueen – an introduction
L30: 
L31:   * Last updated: 17 April 2024
L32: 
L33: Alexander McQueen was one of the most celebrated fashion designers of his generation, known for his highly original designs that married artistry with exceptional technical ability.
L34: Alexander McQueen (1969 – 2010), known to his friends and family as Lee, was born and educated in London. He left school at 16 to become an apprentice on Mayfair's Savile Row – the historic centre of British menswear tailoring – first at Anderson & Sheppard, and then at Gieves & Hawkes, where he learned traditional tailoring techniques. He later worked as a pattern cutter at the theatrical costumiers Angels & Bermans.
L35: At age 20, McQueen began working as a pattern cutter for the avant-garde, London-based Japanese designer Koji Tatsuno, before moving to Milan to join Romeo Gigli, an Italian designer admired for his understated, romantic designs. McQueen returned to London to complete the prestigious MA in Fashion Design at Central Saint Martins. Already a proficient tailor, here he learned how to be a fashion designer, drawing inspiration from London's history, its world-class museums and emerging BritArt scene.
L36: His graduate collection gained him extensive press coverage, and was purchased in its entirety by the influential fashion stylist Isabella Blow.
L37: 【15†Image†vanda-production-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Suit, Alexander McQueen, It’s a Jungle Out There, Autumn/Winter 1997, designed in Britain, made in Italy. Museum no. T.90:1, 2-2011. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L38: McQueen launched his own label in 1992. He was appointed head designer at Givenchy in 1996, succeeding John Galliano. In December 2000, the Gucci Group (now Kering) acquired a majority stake in McQueen's company, and he continued to serve as creative director. McQueen's occasionally stormy relationship with Givenchy ended in 2001.
L40: McQueen's influences
L41: McQueen's work was admired for its highly original blend of subversion and tradition, evident from the outset in his 'Bumster' trousers, sharp frock coats, corroded fabrics, slashed leather and shredded, flesh-revealing lace.
L42: 
L43: > You've got to know the rules to break them. That's what I'm here for, to demolish the rules but to keep the tradition.
L44: 
L45: Alexander McQueen
L46: McQueen's Savile Row training would inform his career: "Everything I do is based on tailoring", he said. This background in precision tailoring, combined with the more improvised dressmaking and draping techniques he learned in the atelier (the highly skilled workshops of couture houses) at Givenchy – paved the way for his innovative experiments with cutting and construction.
L47: > Because I was a tailor, I didn't totally understand softness, or lightness. I learned lightness at Givenchy. I was a tailor at Savile Row. At Givenchy I learned to soften. For me, it was an education. As a designer I could have left it behind. But working at Givenchy helped me learn my craft.
L48: 
L49: Alexander McQueen
L60: On the catwalk
L61: McQueen was known for the dramatic intensity of his fashion shows, inspired by performance art and theatre.
L62: His spectacular catwalk presentations included the likes of VOSS (Spring/Summer 2001), which was centred around a glass box that resembled a padded cell in a psychiatric hospital, Scanners (Autumn/Winter 2003), where models traversed wind tunnels suspended above the runway, and The Widows of Culloden (Autumn/Winter 2006), where the model Kate Moss appeared as an ethereal apparition within a glass pyramid, echoing a 19th-century stage trick, 'Pepper's Ghost【21†'†en.wikipedia.org】.
L63: In 2009, Plato's Atlantis (Spring/Summer 2010) became the first fashion show to be live streamed on the Internet, via fashion website SHOWstudio.
L64: 【22†Image†vanda-production-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Pepper's Ghost of Kate Moss wearing a silk organza dress, Alexander McQueen, The Widows of Culloden, Autumn/Winter 2006. Art direction by Baillie Walsh. Image: courtesy of Baillie Walsh
L65: During his lifetime, McQueen featured in two V&A Fashion in Motion events – live catwalk presentations staged against the beautiful backdrop of the Museum. The first, in June 1999, showcased designs from McQueen's 【23†Spring/Summer 1999 collection】, while the second, in October 2001, celebrated the years of collaboration between McQueen and the jewellery designer 【24†Shaun Leane】.
L66: By then, McQueen's reputation was such that over 3,000 people gathered in the Museum's grand entrance, hoping to see the event.
L67: Collaborations
L68: McQueen worked with a loyal, close-knit team and was known for his ability to recognise talent in others, whether jeweller, milliner or filmmaker. For his spectacular catwalk shows, he commissioned an array of one-off creations, not intended for production. To realise this vision, he worked with a diverse range of materials and craftspeople – from skilled woodcarvers to 'plumassiers' (feather workers), embroiderers to leather workers.
L69: As well as his longstanding collaboration with Shaun Leane, McQueen worked closely with the milliner 【25†Philip Treacy】.

L32: 【15†Exhibition Kimono: Kyoto to Catwalk Ran from 27 August 2020 to 25 October 2020 at】
L33: Japan has a very rich textile history, with the kimono being a major focus of interest and artistic expression. Meaning 'the thing to wear', the term kimono was first adopted in the mid-19th century. Originally worn by commoners, or as an undergarment by the aristocracy, from the 16th century kimono became the principal item of dress for all classes and both sexes. It is still an enduring symbol of traditional Japanese culture today.
L34: 【16†Image†vanda-staging-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 S'Kimono for Women', 1800-50. Museum no. FE.101-1982. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L35: Kimono are simple, straight-seamed garments. They are worn wrapped left side over right and secured with a sash called an obi. The length of the garment can be altered by drawing up excess fabric under the obi. Other adjustments can be made to suit the wearer, such as pulling back the collar so that the nape of a woman's neck can be more sensuously revealed. The wrap style allows for ease of movement - a useful feature for a culture where many activities are performed while seated on the floor.
L36: The kimono is also well-suited to Japan's climate, with unlined kimono worn in the humid summers and multi-lined kimono worn in the winter.
L37: In kimono it is the pattern, rather than the cut of the garment, that is significant. Indications of social status, personal identity and cultural sensitivity are expressed through colour and decoration. Only the elite regularly wore luxurious kimono; the majority of people would only have worn silk garments on special occasions. The choice of obi and accessories, such as combs and pins worn in the hair, are also important.
L38: 
L39: Kimono symbolism
L40: The images used on kimono often have complex levels of meaning. The most popular bird depicted on kimono is the crane. Believed to live for a thousand years and to inhabit the land of the immortals, it is a symbol of longevity and good fortune.
L41: 【17†Image†vanda-staging-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 (Left) Kimono, Japan, early 19th - mid 20th century. Museum no. T.18-1963. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London. (Right) Detail Kimono, Japan, early 19th - mid 20th century. Museum no. T.18-1963. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London.
L42: 
L43: Specific motifs were used to indicate virtues or attributes of the wearer, or relate to the season or occasion such as weddings and festivals where it bestows good fortune on the wearer.
L44: Colours also have strong metaphorical and cultural meanings. Dyes are seen to embody the spirit of the plants from which they are extracted. Any medicinal property is also believed to be transferred to the coloured cloth. Blue, for example, derives from indigo (ai), which is used to treat bites and stings, so wearing blue fabric is thought to serve as a repellent to snakes and insects.
L45: 【18†Image†vanda-staging-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Kimono, 1860-1890, Japan. Museum no. 874-1891. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L46: The introduction of the concept of the five elements from China to Japan in the 6th century gave colours a cosmological dimension. Fire, water, earth, wood and metal are associated with particular directions, seasons, virtues and colours. Black, for example, corresponds to water, north, Winter and wisdom. Colours also have strong poetic significance.
L47: Purple, for example, is a metaphor for undying love, the imagery deriving from the fact that gromwell (murasaki), the plant used to create the dye, has very long roots. Perhaps the most popular colour for kimono is red, derived from safflower (benibana). Red signifies youthful glamour and allure, and so is suitable for the garments of young women.
L48: Natural motifs
L49: 
L50: The richest source for kimono motifs comes from the natural world. Flowers such as peonies, wisteria, bush clover and hollyhocks frequently appear on garments. Many of them, for example cherry blossom, chrysanthemums and maple leaves, have a seasonal significance.
L51: 
L52: 【19†Image†vanda-staging-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Kimono, 1780-1800, Japan. Museum no. FE.106-1982. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L53: Pine, bamboo and plum are known collectively as the Three Friends of Winter (shōchikubai), and are symbols of longevity, perseverance and renewal. The pine tree is an evergreen and lives for many years, bamboo bends in the wind but never breaks, and the plum is the first tree to blossom each year. The plum is particularly favoured for winter kimono as its use suggests that spring is not far away.
L54: Birds, animals, butterflies and dragonflies also appear on kimono, along with other motifs drawn from the natural world such as water, snow and clouds. On some kimono whole landscapes of mountains and streams are depicted.
L55: 
L56: Poems and stories
L57: 
L58: Elements of the natural world that appear on kimono usually have strong poetic associations, while more complex landscape scenes often refer to particular stories drawn either from classical literature or popular myths.
L59: Although such stories invariably involved people, it is relatively unusual to find human figures depicted on kimono. Instead there are objects which suggest their presence or recent departure, a pair of dropped fans, for example, alluding to lovers disturbed.
L60: 
L61: 【20†Image†vanda-staging-assets.s3.amazonaws.com】 Kimono, 1937, Japan. Museum no. FE.2-2005. © Victoria and Albert Museum, London
L62: From the early 20th century increasingly graphic imagery was used on kimono. On garments for young boys, in particular, symbols representing Japan's modernity and progression are depicted - cars, trains, aeroplanes and skyscrapers. In the 1930s such motifs became increasingly nationalistic and militaristic.
L63: 
L64: Find out more in our books, 【21†Japanese Dress in Detail】, and 【22†Kimono: Kyoto to Catwalk】.

L17: Indian sari, 19th century. Copyright Victoria & Albert Museum, London, UK, acc. no. IS.181-1960.
L18: A sari is a woman’s garment made out of a long length of cloth. It is particularly associated with Hindu women living in the Indian subcontinent and among the Indian diaspora. A sari can vary in length from 4 – 9 metres and may be between 60-120 cm wide. This variation is due to regional differences in form, as well as differing methods in how it is worn (depending on the social group of the wearer, daily or ceremonial occasions, dance, etc).
L19: Saris normally have a narrow border along the two long sides and a deep border at one end. Saris are often decorated with printed, woven or 【4†embroidered】 designs.
L20: By the end of the twentieth century, saris were generally worn with a long petticoat and a short blouse (choli) with short sleeves. In order to create the skirt section, the cloth is wrapped around the waist several times, and 4-10 folds of between 5-10 cm in width are made and held in the hand and then tucked into the petticoat at the front of the garment. The cloth is then wrapped around the waist again.
L21: The remaining cloth is normally draped over the left shoulder or over the head coming down over the right shoulder and covering the upper front of the wearer’s body.
L22: There are various types of embroidered saris, which reflect social and regional differences, as well as the occasion when a sari is being worn. The embroidered saris from Gujarat and Rajasthan, for example, use mirrors as part of the design (【5†shisha】 work). 【6†Kasuti†en.wikipedia.org】 embroidered saris have a design made from lines of 【7†running stitch】.
L23: A more subtle form of embroidered saris comes from Lucknow, Uttar Pradesh. This type is decorated in 【8†chikan】 work, a form of 【9†shadow embroidery】. The delicate designs of embroidered saris from the Kashmir region use fine 【10†wool】 or 【11†silk】 for the embroidery. The most elaborately embroidered saris are those used for brides, and such saris are often decorated with metal thread (【12†zari】, zardozi) embroidery of various types.
L24:
